subject: Archaeology
title: The Vindolanda Letters: Voices from the Edge
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Vindolanda Letters: Voices from the Edge usable.

hook.text: Thin wooden tablets found in the mud of northern England contain the personal letters of Roman soldiers and their wives.

buildup.text: Claudia Severa invited her friend Lepidina to a birthday party.

discovery.text: Other letters request supplies: hunting nets, beer, and 'more friends to invite.' Life at the frontier was lonely.

twist.text: One intelligence report calls the local Britons 'wretched little Brits' — an ancient insult preserved by accident.

climax.text: Over 400 tablets have been found, making Vindolanda the richest source of personal Roman writing outside Egypt.

punchline.text: A birthday invitation survived 1,900 years. The party did not.

quiz.question: What is historically significant about Claudia Severa's tablet?
options: It describes the first known Roman military strategy in Britain
It is the earliest known handwriting by a woman in Latin
It contains the only surviving recipe from Roman Britain

details.summary: The Vindolanda tablets are thin wooden writing tablets found at a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall, preserving personal letters, military reports, and shopping lists from around 100 CE. They are the oldest surviving handwritten documents from Britain, revealing intimate details of frontier life.
details.whyItMatters: The Vindolanda tablets humanize the Roman military like no other source. Birthday invitations, complaints about socks, and requests for beer reveal that Roman soldiers were ordinary people managing daily life far from home.
takeaways: Vindolanda tablets are Britain's oldest handwritten documents
They include personal letters, reports, and shopping lists from 100 CE
The tablets humanize Roman military life at the frontier

faq.question: What is the most famous Vindolanda tablet?
faq.answer: A birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, one of the earliest known examples of writing by a woman in Latin. It includes a formal section dictated to a scribe and a personal postscript added in Claudia's own hand — a touching personal touch.

faq.question: How did the tablets survive?
faq.answer: The waterlogged, oxygen-free conditions at Vindolanda preserved the thin wooden tablets that would have rotted anywhere else. Over 1,600 tablets have been recovered so far, with ink writing still legible on many, making them an unparalleled archive of Roman frontier life.
